cards.front: What pretraining qualities must an athlete demonstrate before engaging in a plyometric training program?
cards.back:
To minimize injury risk and optimize performance, an athlete must:
  • Understand and demonstrate proper plyometric technique.
  • Possess a sufficient foundational base of strength, speed, and balance.
  • Demonstrate adequate physical and psychological maturity to follow instructions and respect safety guidelines.

cards.front: What biomechanical alignments define proper landing technique, and what severe injury risk is linked to dynamic knee valgus?
cards.back:
Proper Landing Alignment:
  • Shoulders should be positioned over the knees, and knees over the toes, achieved through synchronized flexion of the ankles, knees, and hips (triple flexion).
  • The center of gravity must remain directly over the base of support.
Dynamic Knee Valgus: Inward movement/collapse of the knees in the frontal plane is a major risk factor for patellofemoral pain and tears or ruptures of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

cards.tag: Strength Prerequisites: Historical Rule vs. Modern View
cards.front: How do modern strength and conditioning recommendations contrast with historical 1RM squat strength prerequisites for plyometrics?
cards.back:
Historical Guideline: Previous recommendations held that an athlete's 1RM squat should be at least 1.5 times their body weight.

Modern Consensus: Technique and movement mechanics are far more critical than an arbitrary strength ratio. Progressively teaching proper alignment, landing, and deceleration mechanics has repeatedly been shown to decrease injury risk during sports competition, making progressive plyometrics safe and appropriate for young and novice athletes.

cards.front: How is balance evaluated prior to plyometrics, and what testing standards apply to beginners versus advanced athletes?
cards.back:
Balance is tested across three progressively challenging tiers (standing, quarter squat, half squat) held for 30 seconds without falling (Table 18.7):
  • Beginner Athlete: Must successfully stand on one leg (single-leg standing) for 30 seconds without falling.
  • Advanced Athlete: Must maintain a single-leg half squat for 30 seconds without falling before starting high-intensity programs.
  • Testing Surface: Must be performed on the exact same surface used for the plyometric drills.

cards.tag: Large Athletes (>220 lbs / 100 kg) Safety Guidelines
cards.front: What training modifications and depth jump height restrictions apply to athletes weighing more than 220 pounds (100 kg)?
cards.back:
Greater body mass significantly elevates compressive impact forces on joint structures. Consequently, athletes over 220 pounds (100 kg) must:
  • Avoid high-volume, high-intensity plyometric exercises.
  • Restrict depth jumps to a box height of 18 inches (46 cm) or less.

cards.front: Which preexisting orthopedic conditions and musculoskeletal histories require extreme caution before initiating plyometrics?
cards.back:
Athletes must be screened for:
  • A history of recurrent muscle strains.
  • Pathological joint laxity (ligamentous instability).
  • Spinal dysfunction, specifically including vertebral disk compression, disk herniation/dysfunction, or structural abnormalities of the spine.

cards.front: What landing surfaces are recommended for lower body plyometrics, and why are thick mats (≥6 inches) and mini-trampolines contraindicated for power training?
cards.back:
Recommended Surfaces: Grass fields, suspended floors, or dense rubber mats (providing adequate shock absorption without excessive compliance).

Surfaces to Avoid: Concrete, tile, and unyielding hardwood lack shock-absorbing capacity.

Thick Mats (≥6 in [15 cm]) & Mini-Trampolines: Cause deep foot sinking that extends the amortization phase. A prolonged transition prevents the stretch reflex from potentiating muscle activity and causes stored elastic strain energy to dissipate as heat.

cards.front: What spatial dimensions and ceiling height clearances are required for plyometric training facilities?
cards.back:
• Running & Bounding Straightaways: Require at least 30 meters (33 yards) of clear straightaway, and up to 100 meters (109 yards) for advanced bounding drills.
  • Ceiling Height: Standing, box, and depth jumps require an unobstructed ceiling height of 3 to 4 meters (9.8 to 13.1 feet).

cards.front: What specifications are required for plyometric boxes and athletic footwear?
cards.back:
Box Specifications:
  • Height range: 6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm).
  • Landing platform: at least 18 by 24 inches (46 by 61 cm).
  • Construction: sturdy 3/4-inch (1.9 cm) plywood or heavy-gauge metal with a nonslip surface (treads, sand mixed in paint, or rubberized flooring).
Footwear: Requires good ankle/foot support, solid lateral stability, and a wide, nonslip sole. Running shoes are contraindicated due to narrow soles and lack of lateral support, which invite ankle inversion injuries.

cards.tag: Depth Jumping Height Standards & Biomechanical Limits
cards.front: What are the recommended heights for depth jumping, and why is a 48-inch (1.2 m) drop height contraindicated?
cards.back:
Depth Jump Heights:
  • Recommended Range: 16 to 42 inches (41 to 107 cm).
  • Standard Norm: 30 to 32 inches (76 to 81 cm).
  • Athletes > 220 lbs: ≤ 18 inches (46 cm).
Contraindication of 48-Inch Drops: A 48-inch (1.2 m) drop imposes an excessive impact load that forces excessive joint flexion, dangerously prolonging the amortization phase, causing stored elastic energy to dissipate as heat, and defeating the neuromuscular purpose of the drill while dramatically escalating injury risk.
